utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that both parties had preliminary matters to be raised. Defence first. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. We have one short policemen matter. Yesterday we were informed by my learned friend Mr. Traldi that this witness was warned that he was actually questioned in relation to Mr. Talic. That warning was on page 74 and 75, and all questions end at page 75. So we just want the position from the Prosecution whether this warning influenced the testimony, previous testimony, of this witness. Because it was put to him that he was warned and that it influenced his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think Mr. Lukic is slightly misstating what happened yesterday. It was put to the witness that he was interviewed in the context of the Talic trial, and the witness discusses at the beginning of the interview, for instance, how everyone in Republika Srpska knows about the summons, that he has spoken to other people he'd worked with and had been interviewed. It was not put to him that the warning itself had caused him to give that particular answer. We did put on the record that he had been informed after he testified that he had not been informed. And so that's our understanding of the actual state of affairs as to what happened yesterday as to what he was told during the interview. As to Mr. Lukic's specific question, of course it's not our position that the warning at the end of the interview influenced answers he'd given before the warning was given. It was put to him that he was aware of the context in which he was interviewed, and it is our position that that may have influenced answers he gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, having heard the position of the Prosecution any further --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are satisfied with this answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That was the preliminary matter raised by the Defence. Prosecution. Two matters, I understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yesterday -- first of all, can we move into private session first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning again. Just to put on the record, on 19 November 2014 the Prosecution informed the parties by e-mail that it had received the complete English translation for P6864 which had been admitted through Witness Kralj on the 29th of October of this year. This was placed on the record on the 25th of November. The complete translation replaced the incomplete version. Defence counsel brought an error in the complete translation to our attention, and the errors has been corrected. A corrected complete translation has now been uploaded into e-court under doc ID 0676-9828b ET, and we would request that the Court Officer be instructed to replace the current translation with the corrected complete translation uploaded under that doc ID number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber instructs the Court Officer to replace the translation which is at present in e-court for P6864 by the newly uploaded document in e-court doc ID 0676-9828b ET.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony. And Mr. Lukic will now continue his re-examination. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have a lot of work this morning. I'm relying on your short answers. P7005 is the next document I would like to show you. Yesterday I wanted to show it to you but I was not sure about the pages. I know that the interpreters in the B/C/S booth tried to help me, but I was on the English channel so I couldn't hear them, unfortunately. In this document, which is a stenographic record of the 8th Session of the Assembly of the Serbian People which took place on the 25th February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call up page 60 in English and page 75 in B/C/S. Paragraph 3 in English on this page, and in the B/C/S version, I'm interested in the last paragraph at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed this to you. You said: "I am against any joint institutions together with Muslims and Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina." What was the sentiment on the 25th of February, four days before the referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was to be held? What was the sentiment on the political scene.

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same when the Serbian deputies were overvoted with regard to the sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina. Again, the constitution was breached, that was our sentiment. We realised that we could not find a common language with them as hard as we tried. Both the referendum and declaration on sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina were against the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is why I said what I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I invite you to slow down when speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm rushing you. At the same time, you do have to speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call up P7006. I apologise. We're finished with that. We're moving on. P7007, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is an excerpt from the minutes of the 10th Session of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. You disputed the contents of this document. You were asked about that on transcript page 29752. You were asked whether Karadzic, Koljevic, Krajisnik, and yourself were legally elected. My question is this: The person that I've just mentioned, were they legal representatives of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was the only legally elected member of the Assembly of Krajina and the president of that assembly. None of the others were -- they were legal representatives of the Serbian people at a higher level, at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I'd like to go back to P2720.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is an intercepted conversation. There's no date. It says that the conversation took place in April 1992. Before we start dealing with the content of the document, let me ask you this: Was there a mistrust at the time between Serbian representatives and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that the Serbian people ever had any doubts about the Yugoslav People's Army, not for a moment. I am saying that based on the platform of my party which was to preserve Yugoslavia at all costs. This failed because of the international community. We did not have any other political projects, unlike other peoples who had their own political programmes and their goal was to break up Yugoslavia as a sovereign state. I'm talking about two different concepts: Muslims and Croats wanted to break up Yugoslavia at all costs, start a war, and sacrifice peace; whereas our concept and our objective was to preserve Yugoslavia. We trusted the Yugoslav People's Army, although the army was slowly withdrewing -- withdrawing from our area and we were left abandoned, and that's why we decided to establish our own military.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the JNA try to export equipment as well?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that some military equipment was supposed to leave Krajina and to be sent to Krajina, and it is true that it did left on aircraft, MiG aircraft were transport to Yugoslavia. We did not allow the rest to be taken because if we had allowed that, the Serbian people would have to leave as well. We stopped the export of weaponry, and we kept the Serbian people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let us look at English page 2, and B/C/S 3, please. In the English version, I'm interested in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There you are recorded as saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same passage is found at the top of the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were recorded as saying that Karadzic was supposed to return from Europe. That's what you said to Kukanjac in April 1992. You said the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the one side and the Serb people in the situation they're in on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let's look at English page 3 and page 4 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is a reference to arming and Kukanjac says: "You have a lot over there." And then you respond: "We have nothing here. And in comparison with our enemies, how many enemies we have? And Grahovo has been attacked. Kupres has been attacked, Glamoc has been attacked, Krupa has been attacked, Sanski Most, Derventa, Samac, Modrica." In April 1992, therefore, did you make this up or were those places indeed attacked and who they were attacked by?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever I said is true. Muslims and Croats had been attacking us for three months from March to May. The first thing that happened, a member of the wedding party was killed in Bascarsija in Sarajevo, and then up -- on the 10th of March, the Croatian army entered Brod and in Sijekovac they killed about 50 Serbs. I'm talking about the village near Brod. They blockaded the road to Modrica, Odzak, Derventa, Doboj, and the road from Derventa to Prnjavor, and they destroyed a very big bridge there. And then the Muslims attacked Serbs in Kljuc in the month of April. They killed six soldiers. They had been demobilised and were on their way to Serbia from Knin. They wounded a lot of people. They destroyed a relay, and in Kljuc they killed a deputy commander of the police. They blew up the Avnoj motorway from Petrovac to Kljuc. And then on Kupres in the village of Balavan [phoen], a certain number of Serbs were killed, and then the Croatian army moved to Kupres and killed a total of 57 civilians there. The process was ongoing. In Sanski Most in the village of Hrustovo, several reservists were killed. There was also a conflict in Mahala, I don't know what happened there. And then on the 22nd of April, six reservists were killed in Hambarine. And also on the 26th of April a soldier was killed in Kozarac. On the 30th of May, Muslims attacked Prijedor. And then from Brod to Odzak, camps were established in Novi Grad. Rapes and murders started. And also at the end of April and the beginning of May, crimes started in the valleys of Bosna and Lasva. Muslims torched Serbian villages and they killed children and infirm. They attacked villages such as Drjusa, as far as I remember, Zeleca where everybody was killed, Perin Han also. Let me try and remember some other villages. As a matter of fact, all the villages on the left and right banks from Zenica to Zavidovici and Maglaj. The Yugoslav People's Army troops were killed in Sarajevo as well as in Tuzla. The process of killing and attacking was ongoing. And then in Posavina on Vucak mountain the Serbian population, women and children, 30.000 of them were expelled. Their delegation came to see me and asked for assistance. I addressed Radovan Karadzic and I sent that delegation by a small helicopter to Pale to see what could be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I thought you were seeking a confirmation that indeed those villages were attacked. Now, do you need all these details? A simple yes, I do understand, is that there were attacks. But if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't mind having all the details since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you do not mind but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- it was personal knowledge of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I do not know. He has not told us anything about personal knowledge about what happened in these attacks. But apart from that, Mr. Lukic, if you say you do not mind to have the details, please be aware of the limited time you have. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned all these places, Mr. Kupresanin. All the places that were attacked. What is the source of your information regarding what you have just told us?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are my sources? My sources are people. The information that I got. Actually, everything I said is true. Perhaps I did not provide the exact detail -- dates. Maybe there are some differences there. But I heard it all from people. At the time the state of Republika Srpska wasn't functioning, so a number of people in certain areas focused on me thinking that I could provide solutions for all problems, even though I didn't have any command responsibility and I couldn't issue orders to the army. It was all about what happened to the population who were in that area; 30.000 women and children. People who came, they were crying. And then after a few days the supreme commander came, Radovan Karadzic, and General Mladic. On that day on the 2nd of June, the decision was made to breakthrough the corridor. People were -- children were constantly dying. Children, babies were dying in the clinical centre in Banja Luka due to a lack of oxygen. We had no way out. We had to breakthrough a passage towards Yugoslavia, and that was when the decision was made to go through the corridor. That is what my story was about. That's what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the fifth page in the English version and page 3 in the B/C/S version. In the English version, it's the fourth box from the bottom. [In English] Third page in English, please. We have to go back. And fifth page in B/C/S. Yes. Third page in English. Fourth box from the bottom on the third page. [Interpretation] And the third boxes from the top in -- on the B/C/S page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin, you tell Kukanjac: "We won't strip you of your rights if you are working for the general well-being of all peoples." At this time, the Serb side -- you say there were constant attacks in March and April and May, so did the Serb side ask the JNA ever to attack the other two peoples?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We did not ask that in any way. What was it that we were preoccupied with? Since Bosnia and Herzegovina had collapsed. We wanted to protect the ethnic territories inhabited by the Serbian people with the forces that we had in order to prevent them from experiencing the same fate as they did in World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Serb politicians at the time, and you were one of them yourself, did they consider this behaviour by the other two sides as anti-constitutional?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew it was anti-constitutional. We knew all of that. We had to do something about it because the Serb people were being vilified at the time. We were proclared [as interpreted] a national -- an ethnic minority and we were constantly being abused. We didn't have any prospects or any future. Muslims and Croats were working on such a project themselves, the international community was party to this project. There was a decision adopted in Rome that Yugoslavia had to die. This was something that was committed by western Europe. Sometimes we blame Serbs and Muslims and Croats, I personally think that none of those three sides wanted to do it. It was just some political leaders who had come to that area to create war and that was the reason for war. Nobody wanted to see their children killed. We were all wise enough to know that war is terrible, but I think that the international community was the one that really interfered in this situation the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you allow again and again the witness to go far beyond what your question is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that you do not might -- mightn't to hear details. Apparently you also do not mind to hear matters which you didn't ask for. But please, it's your time, and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can I have D827 now, please. I'm trying really to speed up this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] without many things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You should intervene once the witness -- if he says it was anti-constitutional, he has answered your question. And then to hear ten lines later what -- whether children were killed or not. I mean, that is very important but it's not an answer to your question. It's far from related to it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kupresanin, we are looking at an issue of the Official Gazette of the municipality of Prijedor. It's issue number 2/1992 dated the 25th of June 1992. I would like to show you something at the end of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to look at English page 98 and B/C/S page 43. Let's look at 116 in the B/C/S. In the English version, we're looking at this number, 116, but the number is on the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A conclusion was adopted on the 23rd of June, 1992. The Prijedor Municipal Crisis Staff concluded that that Crisis Staff does not accept and considers invalid all the decisions of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of the Krajina which were adopted before the 22nd of June, 1992. I am not going to go into whether this was implemented later or not. What I want to ask you is this: Are you aware if anyone from the Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff was replaced because of this?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the whole time, I have been trying to convince this Honourable Court that what the Crisis Staff was doing was unpunished, and all conclusions they attempted to implement could not do it because of the sanctions, and you can see specifically that nobody in Prijedor could implement decisions of the Crisis Staff. However, Prijedor was specific. It was a state within a state. And all the municipalities in their own way were states within states. Who did the Prijedor municipal leadership listen to? They didn't listen to anyone. Not to the political leadership in the Krajina. Prijedor as such, that municipality, was not part of the Krajina region, which means that it's true that the decisions of the Crisis Staff were ultimately not implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. We're not going to go into it, whether they were implemented or not. The question is: Did you try to replace anybody? Did you ever reach a decision to replace the president of the Prijedor municipality Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at a Prosecution document, P4337.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you were talking about the makeup of the Crisis Staff of the ARK.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to look at the top of the B/C/S page. Could we zoom in on that part, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see a decision here about the formation of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of the Krajina. And you are listed under number 3. Out of these 17 people, was anybody a representative of any of the members of the municipality that were part of the ARK?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just looked. There is none. I looked at it yesterday, and what I said then was accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at your interview with the Prosecution marked 65 ter 31770. Since you know what document we're talking about, we won't look at the first few pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need to look at page 68 in the English version and then page 100 in the B/C/S version. I don't know how it happened, but I have the wrong page again. But it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the Prosecutor asking you yesterday about the situation when you were bringing people out of Manjaca? We saw that document about Sejmenovic that you signed. How did this happen? How did it come about that you went to Manjaca and brought out somebody? Who asked you what did you do, who approved it? Could you please tell us briefly.

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not Manjaca. It was the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that's about five questions and not -- not accurately describing that portion of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you split it up, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned Sejmenovic. I'm going to go back to that. Did you bring somebody out of Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I brought Sejmenovic out of Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, all right. But let's go back to Manjaca. Did you bring anybody out from Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received a number of requests to pardon Muslims and Croats who were in the camp at Manjaca or Omarska. Whenever they would come to see me, I would ask them to sit down. I would give them coffee, juice. We would discuss problems, and then I would say write down the names of the people, their first and last name, their profession, they would do that, and I would pass that on to the Supreme Commander of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please don't answer things that I'm not asking you about. So please listen carefully to what I'm asking you. Those people came to you. They gave you the names. What did you do with those names?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I passed those names onto the president of the republic, Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he would answer affirmatively in two, three minutes, or five minutes at the most, and then I would pass that on to the command of the Banja Luka Corps, and then the Banja Luka Corps command would pass it on to Manjaca. That was the procedure in all correspondence regarding the pardons, the abolitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did it ever happen that any Muslim or Croat asked you to bring out any Croat or Muslim from Manjaca and that you refused such a request?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I complied with all the requests. I would go through the Banja Luka Corps, and I know that many times Stevo Bogojevic helped me. He was the chief of the police, and he was willing to respond to all such cases, so I didn't have any problems either with the army or with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us the number, approximately? Are we talking about five or 550 or 300? What's the number of people that you helped to leave Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a matter of fact, I didn't help them. Radovan Karadzic helped them. He was the one who approved these requests for pardon. I don't recall the number of the people now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, it is pretty clear that you asked for people to be released. You don't recall the number? Approximately. I mean, if you say ten, that could be nine or 11. If you say 50, that could be anything between 40, 45, to 55, 60. But what was the approximate number of people that could leave Manjaca due to your intervention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps 20. I don't know, 30, perhaps -- I -- I don't know. I'm not sure about the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you -- do you have, apart from the one, the name you had for Omarska, do you have any names of those who could leave Manjaca through your intervention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did know some names, I'm going to try to remember. I know a young man who was from Sanski Most, but I don't remember his first and last name. I don't remember the first and last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you remember a name, please tell us. Please, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kupresanin, did it ever happen that President Karadzic approved the request and somebody's release and that the army rejected that and did not release that man?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it never happened. The army always complied with such requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now just briefly let's deal with Omarska and the time that you took Sejmenovic out. Who approved his release?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found the head of the camp, I don't remember the first and last name of that person, I know that he was wearing a blue uniform, and all I saw around were mainly blue uniforms. Since he was my deputy, I told the head of the camp that is my wish to meet with all the deputies who just happened to be there. He said that there was one and he said that that was Sejmenovic. I remember his first and last name because we were together for a year and a half in the Serbian parliament. I considered them to be my colleagues and that it was my duty for me to help them to live in better conditions than there were prevailing at that time as far as I could see. So he approved that. I came with him to my office. First of all, I offered to take him with me to my village so that he could fatten up a bit. He was skin and bone. And then he said, I would rather go to Vrbanja to my sister's. I filled a car with food and cigarettes and everything that was needed, and I took him to his sister's place. Then I informed the assembly that I had found Sejmenovic, and the assembly asked to see him. They requested to see him. Milorad Dodik, the president of Republika Srpska, sat with me in the car, Kelecevic, and Mijatovic, and we went to his house. We all greeted him cordially, we spoke with him, and actually I insisted that he becomes a deputy in the Assembly of Republika Srpska, which he refused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you have ten minutes left. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have a lot to cover. Just this: So he refused?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he refused. We gave him money. All of us gave him money so that he could have money and we left, and then we would see him constantly after that. He refused to be a deputy. Later --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Thank you. Let us move on. That is sufficient. In the document that we see before us, the OTP's interview with you in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at page 42 in the English version and page 62 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Prosecution put to you that you changed your statement in the Karadzic trial as compared to this interview that you gave in 2001. Could you please look at line 12 in the B/C/S version here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English version, it's line 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you begin your answer. You say in 2001: "Radovan Karadzic personally never told me that" -- "... personally told me that he had nothing to do with that," meaning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say line 35, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what we heard from the interpreters is not what's on line 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's -- yeah, line 36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I did read the first two lines. It's line -- what I want to say is that Radovan Karadzic told me personally that he had nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is line 37.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then you say, you said: "But I had a sense, I had a feeling that the order didn't come from Brdjanin but that it came from somewhere, someone at the top, but I don't know who from." So in the B/C/S version here you said twice that it was your feeling that it had come from somebody up at the top. Did you know then and do you know today - do you know - who established Keraterm and Omarska?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this was done by the Crisis Staff or the authorities in Prijedor. Now I am convinced that they did that of their own initiative, and the proof of that is when I brought Sejmenovic to my office with me I had a heated discussion --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Just let's leave Sejmenovic for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, let's also try to avoid again that the witness gives us the conclusions of what he found here and there because --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- drawing conclusions is rather for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah. That's why I interrupted him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know Simo Drljaca? Did you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew. I think that he was the chief the police in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what his role was regarding the establishment of Omarska and Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was a key figure in all of that. Not only him, but a whole team of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. Let's move on. You were asked about Brisevo on transcript page 29803, line 25 on. Transcript for this case. Let's see what you said in 2001 in the same interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at English page 63 and B/C/S page 92. We need to look at line 13 in the English version on this page, and in the B/C/S that would be line 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were asked by Mr. Mazhar Inayat: "Now when they told that you the soldiers from the VRS were involved in the crimes, did it occur to you that you should inform General Talic about it?"

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. And then you replied: "No, I informed ministers, the minister of the army, for example. It was Ninkovic. I don't know if it was Subotic." My question is, was this the regular line of reporting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- you read or you were interpreted as referring to a person Ninkovic. But I read "Nikolic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the original -- the original apparently says Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I didn't see that. Yes, okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And therefore the translation is -- well, I do not know --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is wrong translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because these are the words of Mr. Kupresanin so I take it that they were spoken in B/C/S and then it's a translation issue. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We agree that the original says Ninkovic. But regarding the question, I'd object that it's vague. It's not clear whose regular line of reporting is being asked [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. I [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But there are maybe two different matters: First of all, what Mr. Kupresanin said at the time. Second, how it was recorded in B/C/S. And third, how it was translated in English. And finally, who was at such a position at that point in time. And that's four questions to be distinguished. And I expect the parties to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. I can. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly: Was Ninkovic the minister of the army for a while?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a while. But at that time he was not. Subotic was the minister of the army. Then I wasn't sure and I know now that it was Subotic, not Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your regular line of reporting, did it go towards the ministry?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kupresanin, this is all I had to ask you.

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, when you said ministry, your line of reporting, which ministry did you have in mind? Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just want to thank --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kupresanin, for having answered our questions. That was all we had for you.

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I do have a few questions for the witness. I think it's less than ten minutes. I'm in the Chamber's hands as to whether to take the break now or afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would prefer you to put those questions now because the reasons why we usually have short sessions of one hour is, that reason is not at this moment there. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now you testified this morning at temporary transcript page 9 that in April of 1992 there were incidents of conflict in Hambarine, in Kozarac, and involving Serb reservists in Kljuc. The Chamber has received evidence, including evidence from Defence witnesses, that all those events took place in the second half of May 1992. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to object here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, wait one second, please. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that he said that there were continuous fighting in March, April, May. That's what I heard. If it's not recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. -- you -- the objection is that Mr. Traldi misstates the evidence, then you ask the witness to take his earphones off, and then you tell him why you consider him to misstate the evidence. You have done now in the presence of the witness which is not what we expect you to do. Mr. Traldi, in view of what Mr. Lukic just said, could you either rephrase or further clarify your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd rather respond if that's all right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At transcript page 9, line 15, the witness said: "Muslims" -- And I'd ask that he take his headphone off for the remainder of the discussion, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you take off your earphones for a second, Mr. Kupresanin. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At temporary transcript page 9, line 15, the witness said: "Muslims attacked Serbs in Kljuc in the month of April. They killed six soldiers. They had been," and the transcript reads, "demotorised" but I believe it's "demobilised." He says several lines later, line 24 of the same page: "On the 22nd of April, six reservists were killed Hambarine, and then on the 26th," and there's a tilde there I think to fill in the place, but that's where I recall him mentioning Kozarac. So in the case of instances that I referred to, in fact the witness had testified that they took place in April, the Chamber has recently received evidence from Defence witnesses including, off the top of my head, Witnesses Vracar and Milojica, that these events took place in the latter half of May. My question correctly stated this witness's evidence and the evidence before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Line 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of page?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of the same page, page 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This witness started his answer: "Muslims and Croats had been attacking us for three months from March to May..." And then he continues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's -- yes. [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That answer is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All the -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Stop. Stop. Mr. Traldi did not misstate the evidence, although you consider a certain context relevance, which you could have explored in -- no, not in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I could not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you could have asked for that. But the witness specifically told about certain events to take place on a specific date. Now whether that was in the context of a larger and ongoing armed conflict is a different matter, but to that extent I think that Mr. Traldi has put to the witness what happened on the 22nd of April and I think that when Mr. Traldi was referring to evidence the Chamber received, he was not talking about the Chamber receiving evidence on an ongoing armed conflict but on specific incidents such as the killing of persons in Hambarine which, if I remember well, but I stand corrected, was not the 22nd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah. I can vouch it was 22nd of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can find that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine. So therefore -- when then to -- when they make such a -- Mr. Traldi reflected the evidence carefully and now asked the witness to see whether the 22nd of April may be a mistake, and -- I do see that the parties already agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore -- not the objection is denied. Mr. Traldi may proceed. The witness can put his earphones on again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, just to briefly and concisely restate my question, the Chamber has received evidence, and it appears the parties are in agreement, that some of the events that you referred to as happening in April in fact happened in the second half of May 1992, and to cut to the chase, I'd just put to you your recollection of specific dates at this point is not completely clear; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. Kupres was in April, Brod was in March, Kljuc was in April. Sanski Most was in April. Hambarine was in May, as well as Kozarac, as well as Prijedor. I said Brod was in March. The end of April, the beginning of May was the valleys of Bosna and Lasva where Serbian villages were torched from Zenica to Maglaj. That was around that time, yes. I -- I gave you a chronological order, month by month, very correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Moving now to the questions you were asked about detention facilities. Regarding Manjaca, at temporary transcript page 17 today, you said you co-ordinated with Stevan Bogojevic and that he was the chief of police. In fact, Colonel Bogojevic was the assistant commander for security and intelligence in the 1st Krajina Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was chief in the military police, but I don't know much about the hierarchy of command. When I wanted to speak about people in the camp, I turned to him. I submitted information to him, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Regarding now Mr. Sejmenovic, you said among the people that sat in your car with him was someone named Kelecevic. What was Kelecevic's first name?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zlatko Kelecevic, he was a teacher of Serbian from Banja Luka. And the other was Jovo Mijatovic from Zvornik. I don't know what he was. By profession he was a deputy. And the third one was Milorad Dodik, the current president of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm trying to be very efficient. I'd just asked you about one person's first name and I'd ask that you limit yourself to the question. Separately, as the day you went to Omarska you were conveying a message from President Karadzic, and I'd put to you that what you were saying was international press was about to come and he was telling the authorities there, get ready, make sure what they see looks acceptable. The next day, the great majority of prisoners were transferred from Omarska to Manjaca; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when that group was transferred to Omarska. Radovan told me that those people had been in Prijedor. I don't want to use any banalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that they had created a problem --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and he told me, Mr. Kupresanin, you are a man of good standing, maybe you can exert your influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Then you mentioned an issue in Banja Luka that some babies had died as a result of lack of oxygen. Now this is a terrible tragedy, of course, and I don't meant to diminish it, this occurred - so I'm asking a very specific question - this occurred in a period of just a couple of days in June 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. Before June. The operation to break the corridor was launched on the 2nd of June. Before that, in the months of April and May, the babies died without oxygen because there was no communication with Belgrade and nobody else wanted to help us. Not in June therefore but before June. More specifically, in April and March. Certainly in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Very quickly, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 19997.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is an issue of Glas dated the 4th of June, 1992. We see an article that says: "Unless new supplies of oxygen are procured, the lives of babies will be in danger." It's the 4th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And if we could have 65 ter 19998.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And this is Glas just a couple of days later, dated 8th of June. And we see an article, I believe, it's boxed in the top-right corner, saying: "Yesterday, from Belgrade to Banja Luka, the oxygen has arrived." So I'm suggesting to you this was a problem for a couple of days in June. The results were tragic. But as reflected in these articles, it was a problem for a limited amount of time; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. I know better than you. It was my problem. I was supposed to deal with it. Not just me, but all of us who were leading the Serbian people. That's why I decided that the corridor had to be broken through if we wanted to survive. Because of the 30.000 people on Vucijak, in Brod, Vucijak. That was the reason, the motive. We had to do it. We were being suffocated by the international community. The intention was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I -- you don't have to tell that you know better than Mr. Traldi because Mr. Traldi is asking you questions, he is not doing anything. What he does is to put to you newspaper articles which suggest that the problem became urgent at the first day, I think it was the 4th day of June or the 2nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think the publication was dated the 4th and the article was datelined the 3rd, so in early June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that then the problem became very urgent, whereas on the 8th of June it was reported that the International Red Cross and UNPROFOR had -- had managed to -- to -- to provide the oxygen bottles. Therefore, he sees that there is some friction between your explanation and what he reads in this newspaper articles, and that's what he's asking you about, whether you have any explanation as to dates.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Banja Luka, 12 babies were never born or died. On average, two or three were born in Banja Luka. The babies who needed oxygen was low. It was a process that lasted over months, not seven days. Glas was probably belated in bringing news. It didn't happen on either the 1st or the 2nd or the 3rd. Perhaps one baby died on the 3rd. All the other babies died in April and March. But Glas was quite slow in publishing the news about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only about the months. I think the second month was not translated and written down correctly. If you can clarify because I cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps Mr. Traldi you do it. Though I have another problem that we're coming close to the time where -- no, not yet where the -- No, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, you were recorded to say all the other babies died in April and March. Were those the two months you meant to refer to?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that it was during those two months. I doubt that anybody died in June as a result of lack of oxygen. The article was written in June, but it all obviously referred to something that happened before that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter confirms that the witness did say in the month of "May," not the month of "March."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd tender these two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 19997 receives exhibit number P7012. Document 1998 receives exhibit number P7013, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7012 and P7013 are admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And just to focus the limited rest of the examination, I'd understood Mr. Lukic's questions about the Prijedor Crisis Staff decision, which is D827, to focus solely on whether the ARK Crisis Staff dismissed anyone in response, not whether the Prijedor Crisis Staff continued to implement decisions after that date. I understand this was addressed with Witness Mandzic and I'm not going to go back into it if there's no dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's well understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I think you made that clear in the beginning of your question, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Then finally, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 02366, page 77 in the English, page 53 in the B/C/S. This will be the transcript of the 24th Session of the Republika Srpska Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this morning you said the war in Bosnia was caused by members of the international community. Your position in January 1993 was that the war had been necessary for the Serb people to make Bosnia and Herzegovina predominantly a Serb republic; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that Bosnia and Herzegovina should be a Serbian republic. As a matter of fact, we exhausted all of our political means. We didn't have anything else. So when all the political means are exhausted, you resort to conflict and military means.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not start the conflict on the 1st of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I asked you as of January 1993, what you told the assembly was that your position was that the war in Bosnia was necessary for the Serb people to make it a Serb republic. And we see that here. We see you say: "We say that the war in Bosnia -- the war was not necessary in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The war in Bosnia and Herzegovina was necessary. Right now, if we were to count the population right now, there would be over a million Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Bosnia and Herzegovina would be predominantly a Serb republic. Is war necessary in Serbia? It's a horrible thing to say that the war would be necessary in Serbia. If Serbia does not go into the war now, then in five, six years, the Albanians and Muslims will entirely legally overtake the power in Belgrade, along with the Serb opposition. This war was necessary for the Serb people." Your position as you informed the assembly of it in January 1993 was that the war was necessary for the Serb people to make Bosnia and Herzegovina predominantly a Serb republic; right?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then one last question. Is that what you said then, in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps some of it is relevant, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm not talking about relevance. I'm asking you whether the words just read to you were the words you spoke in January 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember when I said this. If I had seen this before, maybe that would have jogged my memory. We did not impose the war on anybody in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We were the ones on whom the war was imposed, and it is probably because of that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, that's not what I'm asking you. You have stated clearly today that what caused the war to happen, that's evidence you gave today, but we're now focusing on what you said in January 1993. Is it that you don't remember the date that you spoke those words, or is it that you don't remember to have spoken those words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember the contents of this. I've not seen this document before, at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So apparently have you no recollection of having said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. President, that -- and Your Honours, that completes my questions. This is the Assembly session P6921 is reserved for, and so we'll just make sure it's part of the excerpts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Traldi. Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got one question for you. You've told us that Mr. Sejmenovic, when you took him out of Omarska, was skin and bones. Did he tell you why he had -- he was in that shape?

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that he had been walking around the forest for a month. It was raining every day. And then he got bored and decided to surrender. That was his story. It was in the month of June and, indeed, it did rain every day. I remember that. I was wondering how he could spend a whole month in the forest. I found his behaviour very strange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I didn't ask you to comment on his behaviour. I asked you what he told you. And you said it was because he had been in the forest and it was rainy. Now, about Manjaca, are you aware of the -- whether sufficient food was provided to those who were kept in Manjaca when you were there? Do you know? If you don't know, tell us; if you do know, tell us what you know.

utterances.speaker: VOJO KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to place where meat was cut for stews. The meat was fresh, fresh beef, and I could tell that it was prepared in a proper way. I don't know how much food there was. I don't know whether there was enough or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you don't know. You don't know whether there was sufficient for those detained in Manjaca? Thank you. I have no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- further questions. Have my questions triggered any need? Not. Then, Mr. Kupresanin, this concludes your evidence. I'd like to thank very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you for having given me this opportunity to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, as you put it. I believe that I have told you a lot. It was all the truth, and I congratulate you and thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to briefly deal with one short matter, that is, associated exhibits for Mr. Kupresanin. In an e-mail dated the 8th of December, the Prosecution communicated it's position regarding some of the associated exhibits tendered by the Defence with the statement of Mr. Kupresanin. We are aware of that. It is typically a kind of a submission which should be clearly on the record, and therefore the Chamber suggests that you file that submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we could -- I'm sorry for interrupting my learned friend. Maybe we could have the same approach as with the documents of Mr. Lukic: So Mr. Traldi and I sit, we formulate all final versions of the documents and the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm quite happy if you find a solution together. At the same time, the 8th of December, and that's -- [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... not use two more documents this gentlemen couldn't recognise during his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I'm happy with any solution you find. At the same time, we want to have a transparent record of the proceedings so therefore you're invited to have it filed as -- the position you at that time communicated to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We'll do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Then we'll take a break. We'll take a little bit of a longer break. May I take it that Mr. Mladic is waiting to enter the courtroom again --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- for the next witness. I take it, Mr. Lukic, that it's perfectly clear to him that this Chamber does not accept any open expression of appreciation of or disapproval with -- any intervention with witness testimony is not accepted by this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, you know that we do our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, no, I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But sometimes for Mr. Mladic, it's not possible to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether it's possible or not --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- control himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we leave that apart for the time being. We'll take a break, and we'll resume at 25 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are. We are calling our next witness, Mr. Lalovic, and my colleague Stojanovic would lead this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then I put on the record that Mr. Mladic is present in court again. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lalovic. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lalovic. Please be seated. Mr. Lalovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You find him to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lalovic, good day to you.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to our customary procedure, I would like you to tell us your precise first and last name in slow words.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Snjezan Lalovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lalovic, at any point in time did you give a statement to General Mladic's Defence in written form; and did you reply to the questions that were put to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please look at document 65 ter 1D01641.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all extra microphones in the courtroom be switched off, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lalovic, I would like you to look at the screen in front of you where you should see a document, and I would like to ask you to look at that document and to tell us whether on this page of that document we see your signature?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lalovic, is it your signature here on this page that we see, and did you also put in the date in your -- by -- in your own hand?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today, after you have given the solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, would you provide the same answers to the questions, the same questions, if they were put to you, according to your best recollection and knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in essence I would. I wouldn't have much to add or to take away.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender the witness's statement, 65 ter 1D01641. That is the statement by Witness Snjezan Lalovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D01641 receives exhibit number D858, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honours, I would like to read the summary of the statement of the Witness Snjezan Lalovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Witness Snjezan Lalovic has a masters in social sciences and is a journalist. When the war broke out he was in his town of birth, the city of Sarajevo, where he worked at Radio Sarajevo. Since he had to flee from Sarajevo he came to Pale, and that is where he got a job at the newly formed radio and TV station. His job was the job of a journalist, and he remained on that job until the rest of the war. The jobs and assignments he had during the war included reporting from the front, covering the political circumstances, and preparing for daily news, radio, and TV broadcasts, processing news received from different news agencies, and he also monitored current political events and meetings throughout the Republika Srpska. He carried out his work in keeping with the editorial policy of the media company where he was employed. In late May 1995, in the sector of Pale where he lived with his family, dramatic information was received that NATO forces would bomb the town and even the civilian targets in the town itself. The bombing started on the 25th of May, 1995, and the witness recalls that the following day he got an assignment to record members of UNPROFOR who were in Pale. He received the assignment from his editor and during those few days he did not have any contact with General Mladic regarding this particular journalist's assignment. On his way to Pale, on the bridge that they had to cross, he noticed two UNPROFOR members who were tied to the bridge railings. Unknown or unidentified uniformed persons were standing next to them, and he asked their permission to record the scene. When he received this permission, he had a short interview with these people, and this was broadcast in the media. After that, those same uniformed persons told him to record members of UNPROFOR at the radio relay facility in Jahorina because there was a danger that that facility might be targeted. So he took the vehicle together with the cameraman and two members of UNPROFOR, where he went to Jahorina. He found another person in uniform with a balaclava on his head. He recorded his news item. And after briefly staying there, they left the facility altogether. On the way back, nobody said anything ugly or did anything bad to the UNPROFOR members. On the way back, also, General Mladic's name was not mentioned, nor were there any comments that all this was being done pursuant to his orders because that would not be an elementary accurate fact. After returning, he made a brief interview with members of UNPROFOR who were accommodated in VRS facilities at Jahorinski Potok, and then he made a news item about it, when he returned to the offices, and this news item was broadcast in the media. During those few days he did not see General Mladic at all anywhere near the prisoners, and he did not notice any abuse, mistreatment, or threats directed at members of UNPROFOR. Your Honours, this is the summary of the statement of Witness Snjezan Lalovic, and by your leave I would just like to put a few questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do. And keep in mind for the next time that a summary should be short. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honour. Could we look at D858, please. And could we please focus on paragraph -- item 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lalovic, you will see paragraph 1 of your statement, and I just wanted to ask you for a brief clarification. We'll just wait until we can see the document in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Next page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at paragraph 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where you say, among other things: "Since I had to flee the city, I arrived in Pale and started working there." The first thing I want to ask you is this: Are you able to remember the date when you left Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I left on the 2nd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What did you mean when you said, I had to flee the town, the city?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: The situation in town was becoming more and more tense. There was shooting in town. Barricades were being erected all around the city. The barricades were set up mostly by people who seemed very dangerous to me. Mostly these were people wearing civilian clothing and carrying weapons. They had revolvers or rifles, at least in the area where I lived. One time I was even asked for identification when I was with my son in my area. These people did not wear any official insignia and were unpleasant, and it was clear to me that these were some sort of paramilitary or parapolice formations, and they did not look nice at all. There were also increasing shortages of food in town. At the time my wife was pregnant. She was expecting a baby, and it was the most logical thing to me that we should leave the town because there was nothing there for us anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now look at paragraph 6 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to approach the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you come a bit please closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 6 of your statement, Mr. Lalovic, you say: "... sometime towards the end of May, where my family lived at the time, we received the dramatic and troubling news that NATO would bomb the town ..." Could you please explain to the Court a little bit how this news reached you, this information about NATO going to bomb the city?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, we did not have any Internet on the radio and television. All we had was something that people didn't even know how to use properly. But we did receive news from news agency, Beta and Tanjug mostly. The news items were arriving continuously about the possibility of bombing. There was more and more disquiet amongst us, amongst the population also, and I think that also officials at that time were signalling that this was an option. The atmosphere was very unpleasant. Just the idea that we could be exposed to bombing by the largest military alliance in the world was not pleasant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you live at the time together with your family; very specifically, in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: It was a weekend settlement, a settlement of weekend cottage, some 700 to 800 metres away from the centre of Pale. If you think of the centre where the church was. Or 300 metres as the crow flies. It was a small weekend cottage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This was May of -- end of May of which year, sir? Paragraph 6, May, which year are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1995. In May 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lalovic, thank you for the clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at this moment we have no further questions for Witness Lalovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Ms. Bibles, are you ready to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lalovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Bibles. Ms. Bibles is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In paragraph 11 of your statement, you describe setting out on the 26th of May, 1995 to film prisoners who were UNPROFOR members in Pale municipality. You further describe finding two UNPROFOR members handcuffed to a bridge railing, and you say: "As I remember, there were two unidentified uniformed men with their personnel weapons next to them." Is it your testimony that there were just two soldiers with the UNPROFOR men on the bridge?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I think I need to explain how things looked, more or less. When I received that task from my editor, I didn't know exactly where those people were. We were told that the bridges could be exposed to a NATO strikes as well as the television building, military facilities, of course, and even some civilian targets. Since in Pale there is only one significant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to stop you there. Could you be -- focus your answer more on the question. The question was whether it's your testimony that there were just the two soldiers, and explaining to us what rumours were there before it all happened is not needed to answer that question. Could you tell us were just the two soldiers with the men on the bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just coming to that. When we arrived at that bridge, and that bridge is some 700 to 800 metres away from the television building, on that bridge I saw what I thought were two soldiers or armed men. I don't know who they were. They were very far. And I also two UNPROFOR soldiers who were chained or handcuffed to the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In paragraph 11, you also describe asking for permission to film these men and that you gained their approval. Is it your testimony that these men spoke with you freely and of their own will?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: It was only natural that they were frightened. We were also frightened, needless to say. I didn't force them to give me any statement. One of the two people addressed them. My English is very basic. People started gathering. It became noisy. A few minutes later there were more than just those two men, and he told them something along those lines: You need to give a statement. I put a question to an UNPROFOR member. I believe that he was from Ghana, if my memory serves me well. He provided the answer he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd like to play --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, before we put any further question. You said he told them something along those lines. Who is "he" in this context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of the members or, rather, one of those armed people who were there guarding them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you believe that he may have been a VRS soldier from Canada, the man who spoke with these men in English?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know whether he was a VRS soldier because they did not have official VRS insignia, as far as I can remember. And I really don't know whether he was from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, the reason I'm asking you these questions --

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: He spoke Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Okay. The reason that I'm asking you these questions is that this Chamber has considered the evidence of Griffin Evans in which he describes that on 26th of May, 1995, he and another UNPROFOR colleague experienced many difficult things. At one point he describes that they were handcuffed to a bridge in Pale where they were threatened by many soldiers. Evans specifically described seeing you speak with a VRS soldier that he identifies as being Canadian, and then being told by that same Canadian soldier that he was to make a statement for Pale TV in which he was to accuse NATO of bombing civilian targets. He describes being threatened with harm if he said something different than this, and then he was interviewed by you. Do you stand by at this time knowing those facts the voluntariness of the statement that this witness made to you on tape?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I only asked which one of them would give the statement, which one of them would speak. And then I was told that a soldier from Ghana would give a statement and -- and answer questions. I don't remember his name. And as for the atmosphere, it was really heated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, could you assist me in -- you asked the witness about whether the statement was given voluntarily. I think the witness didn't answer that question. He only said that he did not force them to give that statement. He didn't express himself on that. So I'm wondering what you seek confirmation of, where the witness had not answered that question?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I believe I was perhaps going further than I need to with respect to his statement in paragraph 11, where he indicated he asked for permission and gained approval suggesting the voluntariness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. That is a suggestion the witness -- Did you personally ask for permission, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I first arrived there, I introduced myself as a journalist of Serbian TV, and I asked the armed men approval to record the image of the people who were handcuffed to the bridge. And they said that I could. And later I also sought approval to talk to them, to take a statement from them, because it seemed to be of some significance for television. And then after some discussion, they told me that the gentleman from Ghana would, indeed, give me a statement.
