utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd like to play about 30 seconds of a video. That's P2556. And after the video --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, Ms. Bibles, reading paragraph 11 it seems pretty unclear, but perhaps the matter has been verified by now. Who gave that permission? Reading paragraph 11 in full context, it is not the interviewed persons apparently. And in your question you suggested, or at least you drew a conclusion from 11, that it would have been the interviewed persons who would have given their permission, which is -- at least I do not find in paragraph 11. Rather, the contrary. So to that extent it misrepresents a certain sense the evidence as we find it in the statement. But the witness has clarified it that he obtained permission from the two armed men who were with the UNPROFOR soldiers. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could now play, Your Honour, P2556. We'll play from 3 minutes, 3 seconds, to 3 minutes, 38 seconds. And we have played this previously. I don't believe there's any need to play it twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at it. And the transcripts have been provided to the booth?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes. There's not much in the way of audio that's of meaningful value; but yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, first, do you recognise yourself in this footage?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Are you the man wearing the brown jacket?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And all of the footage that we've seen here, is this the bridge upon which you conducted the interview?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And the man who is kneeling down talking to Evans, is this the individual that you've been -- that you were describing, is he the one you obtained permission from?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I see a few individuals in this still. When we arrived there, there were only two. He talked to those men probably about what they should say. I --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: And he could have been the one in charge of the exchange between myself, and there's another journalist there, and those men who were handcuffed to the bridge because his command of English was good.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, sir, I'd lake to move on now to paragraph 13 where you describe that you finished this filming, and I believe you've -- it's been mentioned this morning that you were directed. I believe the quote is: "Later one of the uniformed men told me that we should film a member of UNPROFOR at the radio relay facility on Jahorina because there was a chance that NATO aircraft would fire on this facility." You then describe being given an ATV. So is this the same day, the 26th of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, it was not an armoured vehicle. It was an all terrain vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: And it was on the same day, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, ATV, I meant "all terrain vehicle," not "armoured vehicle." I think that was my mistake, sir. But was it the same day? I guess that's the point I'm trying to make. Do you recall actually doing two interviews at this radio relay facility, one on the 26th of May and one on the 27th of May?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: No. The only interview I conducted was on the 26th of May. When that thing happened on the bridge, on that same [as interpreted] we went to the radio relay station or whatever that was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, sir, you specifically describe that the UNPROFOR men were from Poland and Brazil; correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you, sir --

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Actually one -- yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, the Trial Chamber has heard from UNPROFOR members about being filmed at Jahorina. They have heard from Colonel Kalbarczyk, that he was taken to this location twice. The first time was on the 26th of May with an UNPROFOR member, a Canadian. He then identifies that the next day he was taken to Jahorina and interviewed again with an UNPROFOR member from Brazil. Does that refresh your memory, that perhaps there were actually two times that interviews were conducted at Jahorina?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I was with them only once, and there were also UNPROFOR members from Brazil and there was a member from Poland. I don't know whether he was Polish. But he told me he was a Pole, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to go finally to paragraph 6 of your statement. And paragraph 9. In paragraph 9 of your statement, you say, with respect to filming the UNPROFOR individuals: "In addition, these reports were supposed to serve to fend off further NATO bombings." Now this Trial Chamber has considered testimony and documents relating to this time-period that are fairly extensive; specifically, they have considered the testimony of General Rupert Smith as well as documents that were created during this time-period regarding communications between General Smith and Ratko Mladic on the 26th of May, 1995. In two of these communications, one was a message and one was a phone call that General Smith had with Ratko Mladic, Ratko Mladic refers to killing UNPROFOR members on TV. Now you would agree that you would have been one of the TV reporters with the -- with the UNPROFOR individuals that day; correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I did not understand you. If I understood you properly, you mentioned killing UNPROFOR members? Is that what you said? Is that --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Perhaps I -- perhaps --

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes. The communications that this Trial Chamber has considered in the testimony is that Ratko Mladic advised General Smith that if NATO continued their bombings, that he could watch TV and watch the killing of UNPROFOR members. Now would you agree that you were with UNPROFOR members at sites that would have been NATO targets on the 26th of May, 1995, then?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I was with them. And I could have been killed together with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: So, sir, finally with respect to paragraph 9 of your statement, would you agree when you refer to the fact that the TV reports, your reports, were supposed to serve to fend off further NATO bombings, that this means that the United Nations Military Observers were taken in order to influence the actions of NATO; specifically, to stop them from bombing VRS locations. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I suppose that it would have been logical.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Well, that's what you mean in your statement in paragraph 9; correct?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Not just that. We were with them especially on Jahorina for a very short period of time because we saw NATO aircraft flying over, and we were afraid that we could become their target. They left the area very quickly together with us. Actually, it was a trick. It was a ploy to show that they're up there so that people would seek shelter and move to a safer place.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have one or two questions for you. The last question that was put to you by Ms. Bibles is answered in, what is for me, a bit of an ambiguous way. You said it was a trick. It was to show that they are, so that people could seek shelter and move to a safer place. Now in your statement, you give two aims for the reporting: One was to inform the public, the general public, and I understand that it would be for the general public to seek shelter and move to a safer place. But you also said: "In addition these reports were supposed to serve to fend off further NATO bombings." Do you still stand by that second purpose, as you mentioned it in your statement in paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: In the first part of your question, you say that my objective was to inform the people that we removed them. It was not about them being removed from somewhere. The objective was to show them being tied to certain targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I thought I just repeated your words and your statement. But focusing now then on the second part of my question, do you still stand by your statement where you say that these reports were supposed to serve to fend off further NATO bombings; that is, to convince them that they shouldn't bomb those places where UNPROFOR people were kept and tied?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: We were exposed to the bombardment of the biggest military alliance and those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, please an answer to my question: Whether you still stand by that the purpose, the other purpose of these reports was to ensure that there would be no further NATO bombings.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I can't answer by just yes or no. I have to tell you that every piece of informations has a message to convey, and the message of that piece of information was, inter alia, to fend off NATO aircraft and to prevent them from targeting Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. By showing those UNPROFOR people and suggesting that they might hit their own people. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Them and myself equally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Then I have one final question. You said in paragraph 21: "I did not see any abuse, maltreatment, or threats against UNPROFOR members. Tying someone or chaining them to a bridge, is that included in not seeing any abuse, maltreatment, or would you say apart from them being chained to or -- as you didn't see any other maltreatment, or do you consider this not to be maltreatment or abuse, to chain someone to a bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will all agree that handcuffing anybody to anything was one sort of ill-treatment. When I say that there was no ill-treatment, I meant that nobody beat those people, that nobody physically ill-treated them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear to me now. I have no further questions. Mr. Stojanovic, any questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lalovic, to the best of your recollection how much time did you stay on the radio relay hub on Jahorina together with those UNPROFOR members?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't stay there long. I can't tell you that it was either five or ten minutes because I can't remember. But we were there for a very short period of time. We wanted to leave as quickly as possible because above us, and you will see it in the recording, NATO aircraft were already flying. And we were afraid. We were really scared. So we thought that it was in the best interests of all of us, of us and the people who were with us, to leave as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will finish with the question that was suggested to me in the meantime. That facility where you shot that video-clip, did it end up being destroyed by NATO?

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that it was later hit and destroyed. I don't know whether it was that same facility or a facility nearby because I believe that there were several towers. I don't know whether that one was hit or some other, but I know that I saw a video-clip depicting that facility being destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lalovic. On behalf of the Mladic Defence team, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One last question to you. Unless Ms. Bibles would have any further questions. If you said we were afraid to go there to Jahorina at all, why didn't you stay inside somewhere where you were safe? Why did you go there anyhow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my assignment. I was to record UNPROFOR members, those who were chained to those facilities, and I was supposed to carry out that assignment to accomplish it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any further questions? This then concludes your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just have a few questions. Further questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, I'm not quite clear I understand what you're saying, sir. In paragraph 13 you say that: "Then he brought two UNPROFOR members, gave me an all-terrain vehicle, and told me to go with them to the top of Jahorina and film a conversation with them." Now you're getting instructions here from one of the two soldiers who were on the bridge to take these two people who were tied to the bridge to the top of Jahorina. That was not your original mission. Your original mission was to come and film what was taking place on the bridge. Now, it looks to me like now you were doing the job of the soldiers. First they give you a car, and then they ask you to take two people to the top of Jahorina, and at the top of Jahorina you find somebody in a balaclava who is expecting you. So you were running -- at this point you were running an errand for the police; is that correct? You were not filming what you found them doing. You are causing the people to do something so that you can film them.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: That is not correct. First of all, it was not my assignment to record UNPROFOR soldiers on the bridge. I didn't know they were at the bridge. Only once I left the building while I was looking and assuming, because that was the only important bridge in Pale, I went to that bridge. It wasn't my assignment to go to the bridge because I didn't know where they were. Secondly, when those people were, brought the Brazilian and the Pole, and we got there in a small vehicle -- and as far as I know the road to Jahorina is a macadam road and our small vehicle couldn't have covered that road, and I wasn't sure of the road to Jahorina anyway. They gave us a vehicle where two members of UNPROFOR were placed, and there was an UNPROFOR vehicle of those people who were in the vehicle. So I didn't go there because of them. I did go with them but I didn't drive these people around Jahorina. Thirdly, the things that they told me, that I considered to be information and not any kind of order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. There are two things I would like to show you. In paragraph 8 of your statement you say: "The following day I was given a task by the editorial desk to film prisoners of war who were UNPROFOR members in Pale municipality." As a result of that, you travelled to Pale and got to this bridge. When you got to this bridge, this is what you say in your own statement -- just listen to me.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I was in Pale already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fair enough. But then when you got to this bridge in paragraph 13 you say: "Then he brought two UNPROFOR members, gave me an all-terrain vehicle, and told me to go with them to the top of Jahorina and film a conversation with them." You are being told this by the soldier on the bridge, and he is actually giving you an all-terrain vehicle to do so. And then return them here. You're supposed to return them to him.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I told you why he gave me an all-terrain vehicle, because we came in a luxury car, sedan, and that car would not be suitable for the macadam road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. And he was sending you.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: We couldn't fit ten or more of us in one vehicle. And he informed me that they would -- they could have been placed in a different vehicle, but they put them in the vehicle where the cameraman and I happened to be in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me stop --

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: I mean, they could have been put in a vehicle that was behind us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me stop you. I'm not concerned about the car. I'm concerned about the errand you are doing. The errand you were undertaking from the bridge to the Jahorina top was an errand that you were given by the soldiers on the bridge, not by your editorial -- not your editorial staff.

utterances.speaker: SNJEZAN LALOVIC
utterances.text: No. That was information that they gave me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I have no further [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was information that I received. And on the basis of that information in the same way that I received information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Witness. Witness, first of all, I think Judge Moloto had thanked you for your answer. May I draw your attention that the language of paragraph 13 is quite different. It is not they informed me that they would go there and there, but the language is told me to go with them to the top and then return them here, which means that you are giving instructions on what to do and to deliver the UNPROFOR members back to where you had taken them from. That language is not fully consistent with the evidence you are giving today. Any comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that is a matter of interpretation. I gave the solemn declaration here that I would speak the truth, and what I have told you is how it was, and, in any event, this is something that the footage confirms as well. I didn't go up there independently, I did have an escort of armed persons, and I did not drive people upon anybody's orders but pursuant to information that they would be up there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we'll stop you there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Indeed is a matter of evaluation of the evidence. I do agree with that. You've answered my question. You have brought to our attention that you have given a solemn declaration and you have told us the truth. I add to that that you have, after having given that solemn declaration, also attested to the truthfulness of what is in your written statement. But that sufficiently clarifies the issue. Any further questions? No further questions. Then this concludes your testimony, Mr. Lalovic. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, and I hope that my testimony has contributed to shedding light on some situations that are of dispute, and I hope it has contributed to the work of the United Nations, and I believe that the United Nations is still the highest placed body in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm not -- yes. I'm -- it's appreciated what you said, although we're not used to listen to even short speeches, but I think you tried to use nice words. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it would be best to take the break first and then start the testimony of the next witness after the break. We will resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the next witness be escorted in the courtroom. That next witness would be Mr. Jesic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. No protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll wait for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jesic. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Jesic. Mr. Jesic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. You find him to your left. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir. Could you please first give us your full name so that it can be entered into the record.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: My name is Marijan Jesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask for 65 ter number 1D1699 to be called up in e-court. And I believe we have a hard copy for the witness, if that could be provided to him with the help of the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us if you recognise the signature that we see on the first page of this document?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can please turn to the last page in e-court in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, we have a signature on this page. Can you tell us whose signature is visible here?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: It's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you recall after -- after signing the statement, did you have an occasion to read and review the same in the Serbian language, check, and see if everything is accurately reflected in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had the opportunity to read it, and I pointed out certain errors that I found here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We'll go through them one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd first like to look at page 3 in both languages and paragraph 11. If I can -- actually, I think we have the statement of the last witness up on the screen. If I can have -- I'll check to make sure this is 1D1699.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What we have on the screen now is the previous witness, but ... there we have the statement of the present witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can to page 3 in both versions of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 11 of the same, what correction do you wish to make in relation to the location you were first dragged to?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: About the location of the mechanical engineering school, but actually it's the teachers' school of economy -- economics.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if we can look at paragraph 13 on the next page of both versions of your statement, do you have a correction as to the name of the canal that is referenced in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: I do have a correction, yes. The name of the canal is Berek with a K, not Bereg with a G.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if we can look at paragraph 18 which can be found on page 5 in both languages. Here, sir, you identify two uncles named Radulovic that perished in Jasenovac. Do you have additional information about either your own relatives or your wife's family that also perished in Jasenovac?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would add to my uncles -- with the Court's leave, I have a list in my pocket, it's a long list, so if I'm allowed to take it out or I can provide it, submit it to the Court, the list that I wrote out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you wait for a second. Mr. Ivetic, you were seeking for the witness to present that list or?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct. It's a list of family members by name and date of birth that perished in Jasenovac. We can either have the witness read them into the record or provide the handwritten list to the Court, whichever is Your Honours' preference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, yes. The usual way, of course, is that you would tender that list and then perhaps then ask the witness. Perhaps it's best to put the list on the ELMO, that it will be returned to you, that you upload it into e-court, and that you then tender it. That seems to be the most appropriate way of dealing with it. Could the usher assist in using the ELMO so that we can have a look at the list. If you would give the list, Witness, to the usher, then the usher will put it on the ELMO. Yes. Mr. Usher, could you move it up so that we can see whether we have the whole of the list or whether we have -- I'd say move it a little bit -- yes, zoom out. That's also a solution for the -- zoom out so that we can see the whole of the document. Yes. And would you be now so kind to turn it so that we can also see the other side of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But there is more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then the back of this document, because there appears to be some text on it as well. What is on the back of this document as we see it now on our screen, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Cousins that died in Jasenovac: Stana, Stoja, Kosa, Stevanja, Bosicka, they were all Trivics. And then on the right side, Branko, Mikailo, Ostoja, Stojan, Slavko, Djuro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now what we saw on the other sides, on the yellowish part of the paper, what is found there? And perhaps we can have a look at ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can look at the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What have you written down there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here my father Milan Mile Jesic, born in 1929, he died in 2012, and these are his relatives, uncles and cousins who died in Jasenovac: Pero Jesic, born in 1804, died in Jasenovac in 1942. Then Janjetovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jesic, you don't have to read it all. I take it that you made a mistake --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- when you said 1804. It looks to me as if it's 1894. And then you say these are family members. Some of them have died -- your father died in 2012. There some others are -- are -- have died in 1942. And then the last four lines, could you tell us what we find there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The surname Jesic is from the same line as the surname Janjetovic, but they decided themselves after World War II about who will take up the last name Jesic and who will take up the last name of Janjetovic because the records of the registry of birth were burned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could we now have a look at the other yellowish where we looked already at the back. You don't have to read it all out, but I see for under number 1 there seems to be reference to a person who may have been born in 1885 and died in 1942; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then I similarly see apparently what to seems to be a relatively young child born in 1939, died in 1942. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under number 3, we find another person which seems to have been born in 1928. And could you tell us what was the fate of that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those people were taken out of the column out of the Jasenovac camp, and then they were taken again to forced labour by the Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, first of all could you speak in the microphone. And when you say they were taken out of the column, what -- at what -- in what year did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This happened in 1942.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the documents together give a short family history with when people were born and when they were died -- when they have died, part of them during the Second World War and part of them only in the 1990s of the last century. Is that correctly understood? Then would you mind that it be given to the Defence so that it can be uploaded in electronic format so as to become part of the record of this trial, if the Defence decides to tender them? You're nodding yes. That means that you give your consent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I consent, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please give it to the Defence. I take it that the originals may be returned later on to the witness, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. I will scan it, have it sent to CLSS to get a translation, and then upload both and return it to Your Honours. Should we reserve a number for that, though, or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, let's wait until --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Wait. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the witness has explained what it is. These are his personal notes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jesic, apart from the modifications and corrections that we have just gone through in court, do you affirm that everything else in your statement is accurate as written?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you today some questions on the same topics as in your statement, would your answers in substance be the same as in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Since you have taken a solemn declaration today to tell the truth, can we take it that your answers as written in the statement are truthful in nature?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are truthful. Only truthful.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours the Defence would tender 1D1699 into evidence as a public exhibit. There are no associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D01699 receives exhibit number D859, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D859 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honours, I have a short summary of the witness's statement to be read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The witness was mobilised as a member of the TO in the beginning of 1992 and was tasked with distributing food with a truck. On 30 May 1992, the witness was delivering food on his normal route when Muslim units attacked the city of Prijedor. The witness saw a dead military policeman at the reserve officers' club where strangely he saw no one else when on previous days everyone would come to the truck when he arrived. On his way back to the airport, he passed by the Prijedor SJB and saw three or four dead persons. An armed man in uniform with a green ribbon around his head fired at the witness, hitting the witness and causing him to fall out of the truck. Thereafter, the Muslim soldier shooting at him dragged the witness to the vicinity of the schools where another person was lying on his stomach. Another Serb was then brought and their hands tied behind their backs. None of the Muslims provided medical assistance to the witness. As the Muslims took them through a park towards the bridge over Berek canal, they received incoming fire. After crossing the canal, the Muslim soldier fired again on the witness. Thereafter, the wounded witness was rescued by Serb forces. The witness says Serb people in Prijedor feared the same thing would happen to them in this war as happened in Jasenovac when several of the witness's relatives were killed. That completes the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to look at paragraph 13 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That should be found on page 4 of both the languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now in this paragraph, where this is all happening, you say it is a part of the city predominantly inhabited by the Muslims. Can you tell us if this part of the city was called by any other names, referred to by locals by any other names?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: Yes, Stari Grad. It is true that it was inhabited by Muslims. 99 per cent of the population there were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we could turn to page 5 in both languages, I'd lake to focus on paragraphs 18 and 19 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you have identified persons that were -- that perished in Jasenovac. Can you clarify for us who it was that killed them during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Because as you will see in the list that I have provided to the Trial Chamber, that my mother-in-law survived the ordeal. The people who did that were Ustasha, the military of the independent state of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And geographically, how far is Jasenovac from Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: About 40 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now you've detailed for us the personal toll that your family and your wife's family experienced in Jasenovac. How did that compare to the experience of others in Prijedor of Serb ethnicity during World War II?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: If we're talking about the experiences of the people I am surrounded with, all of them either know or knew somebody who was killed in Jasenovac. As I've told you, Prijedor is some 40 kilometres away from Jasenovac. However, my relatives live even closer, at some 25 kilometres from Jasenovac. And my wife and her family live about 12 kilometres away from Jasenovac. So very close.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, why did the Serb people of Prijedor fear the same thing would happen to them in the war that occurred during the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: A war was in the offing, and they feared the repetition of the scenario from the Second World War. And I am talking about my friends, the people that I had spoken to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn to page 3 of your statement and look at paragraph number 11. At the time that you were fired upon when you were in your vehicle by the Bosnian Muslim soldier, were you armed?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while you were in the custody of the Bosnian Muslim soldiers going through the various locations in Stari Grad leading up to the canal, did you hear or see evidence of any combat?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Close by, very close to the school where we were kept, the three of us had been brought to a classroom and we found two other people already there, there was constant shooting all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How long did your ordeal last? That is to say, how long were you in the custody of these Bosnian Muslim soldiers in and around Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you exactly how long. Approximately half an hour, up to an hour. When we were first captured, we were prostrated on the plateau before the teachers high school, and then for about an hour, up to an hour we were tied in the machine engineering school. And then as they were withdrawing towards Berek and Stari Grad, they used us as a human shield. They dragged us along facing the side from which Serb soldiers were shooting, and that may have lasted for up to an hour. And then when we arrived at Berek and when a Muslim soldier ordered me to cross the canal, their soldier crossed before me, and as I was crossing, that soldier turned around and fired a bullet into my head. From then onwards, I don't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Given your earlier corrections, is it still the engineering school or the school of economics? I see you're referring to the machinery school here, engineering school.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we were first captured, I was taken in front of the school of economics on a plateau there where we were guarded by three soldiers, and then we were transferred to the machine engineering school, to another classroom. And there we found two other men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, where did you undergo medical treatment for your injuries and how long did the treatment and recuperation from those injuries last?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, is that not already in the statement? I remember two years, Belgrade. Or in the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I apologise. I see that on the last page, so I do not need to ask that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll then just end by thanking you, Mr. Jesic, on behalf of General Mladic and the rest of my team, for answering the questions we posed to you today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now that completes our direct examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where in your head did the bullet strike you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here. That's when I was crossing the Berek canal, and before that two bullets I had in the back, one directly in the spine where it shattered, and I have about 50 pieces of shrapnel in the cervical part of the spine. I was also wounded in the left arm, in the left shoulder blade, and I suppose that that was the reason why I fell out of the truck. But I would also like to say that the bullet that hit me here and where about 8 centimetres of my jaw are missing, that was while I was crossing the canal and that's when the Muslim soldier shot me. He [Realtime transcript read in error "I"] simply turned around and fired at me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have a very short question for you. You describe in your paragraph 15 of your statement how your body was still half in the water and that you were lying on your stomach and that you heard a strong detonation, and then you said: "I saw a Serb tank fire a shell." What should I -- I'm trying to imagine what it looked like. You are lying half in the water, under a bridge, and where did you see that tank? Did you see that -- was that very near to where you were or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That passage to Stari Grad is actually connected to a bridge. On the side of the bridge where the entrance to Stari Grad, there are two buildings as wide as the bring. That tank arrived at the bridge and fired a round. I was in the water below the bridge, some 10 metres from the shore, so I could see it. That bridge is not high because it's over a canal, so that bridge is not very high above the water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the Serb tank was very close to where you were, and you were more or less in the midst of combat activity, is that -- was that the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I may one intervention for the transcript. I'm told at temporary transcript page 72, line 25, the witness said "he turned around and shot me," whereas the transcript reflects "I turned around and shot me."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that what you said, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please -- Mr. Jeremy, if you're ready. Witness, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Jeremy. Mr. Jeremy is counsel for the Prosecution. You find him to your right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Mr. Jesic.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now in paragraph 2 of your statement, you refer to your mobilisation at the beginning of 1992, and you say your unit was based at the Urije Sport Aviation airport. Now at this time what was the name of your unit?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And within the Territorial Defence, the unit didn't have any particular name; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And did you have a commander within the Territorial Defence that you immediately reported to?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: Yes, we had a -- a -- a superior officer who was in charge of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And what was the name of that superior officer?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. The -- the commander of the entire Prijedor TO, Territorial Defence, at this time was Major Slobodan Kuruzovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: I don't know. He was not at the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, from late May onwards, your Territorial Defence unit formed -- or became part of the 43rd Motorised Brigade; is that correct? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: From late May? I was wounded on the 30th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: All right. So you're not aware of your TO unit becoming part of the 43rd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: All right. Now, the Urije airport where you were based, that's just to the north-east of Prijedor town; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And while you were based at the airport, there was also a tank brigade based there. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, in paragraphs 4 and 6 of your statement you refer to collecting food from a barracks. Now the barracks you're referring are the Zarko Zgonjanin; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And while you were performing these duties you were wearing a military uniform; yes?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, today you've confirmed that at the time that you were injured you were in a place in Prijedor called Stari Grad. Now, this Chamber has heard evidence that on the 30th of May, 1992, so the date, the same day that you were injured, the VRS attacked Stari Grad, rounded up non-Serbs, and took them to Trnopolje, and then destroyed the mosque in Stari Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And that evidence can be found at P3414, paragraph 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware of these events that occurred on the same day of your injury?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Now in your statement, and it's paragraph 17, you say that after you returned from your treatments you were under a work obligation. Now, is it correct that this work obligation was your -- your work with the veterans' organisation?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And this veterans' organisation was in Prijedor; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, you say in your statement that you received treatment in Belgrade for around two years. So would that therefore mean that you returned to Prijedor in May or June 1994?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: Yes. That would be that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, by the time you returned to Prijedor, the overwhelming majority of the non-Serb population were gone. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I really didn't know that. I did not go into other houses. Around my house or, rather, around the houses of my parents, there were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please take a look at P3853 in connection with the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And while it's being brought up, I can tell the Court and the witness that this is an overview of data on the number and ethnic structure of the population according to the municipalities in the area of Banja Luka State Security Department for 1991 and 1995. The document is dated February 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And could we please go to page 6 in each language.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, sir, referring your attention to number 9, Prijedor, we see that in 1991, the document lists there being 47.745 Serbs; and for the Muslims, 49.454; and for the Croats, 6.300. And if we look to the numbers for 199 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we look to the numbers for 1995, we see that there are approximately 61.000 Serbs; 3.600 Muslims; and 1.000 Croats. So, sir, by 1995, on the basis of these numbers over 50.000 Muslims and Croats had left Prijedor. Now is it your evidence that you didn't -- you didn't notice that -- that many people, that many non-Serbs had left Prijedor by 1995? And to be fair to you, I initially asked you when you returned in 1994; therefore, perhaps by 1995 you had noticed that over 50.000 non-Serbs had left?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: If we're talking figures, I don't know that there were that many or that there were that many Serbs. I'm looking at these percentages here, and as far as 1995 concerns, I was not there at the time. I don't know whether they left or whether they left in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So you're saying that you were not in Prijedor in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. As I'm reading this paragraph, under b, 1995, only 3600 Muslims were left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Jeremy, the witness testified that he didn't go out to other houses, so he only describes the situation in the immediate vicinity of his own house which, of course, is not caught by any percentages or statistics. So the one and only question that really remains then is: You really stayed close to where you were living, and you were, as you told us, not aware of any changes in the population in a wider ranger in Prijedor, Witness? And it's me who is asking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Let me tell you, when I arrived in Prijedor there was no electricity, there was no water, there was no heating. And movement around the city was actually next to none. Nobody moved around, either Serbs or Muslims. The civilians really moved around Prijedor very little. There were few and far between.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, the only thing we're interested in is whether you moved, whether you stayed at home and did not observe anything else than what was next to your own -- to your own home. Is that how we have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, Mr. Jeremy, perhaps statistics would not be of great assistance. And for the witness to start interpreting them is certainly not assisting us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, Witness, so that I understand your answer to the Presiding Judge's question correctly, it's your evidence that when you returned to Prijedor in 1994 you essentially remained in your home or in the immediate vicinity of your home until the end of the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And the -- the duties that you performed as part of your obligations, your work obligation in the veterans' organisation, you performed those from your home; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: No. When I was needed and when they called me, I went to the veterans' organisation to prepare those who were wounded and needed to go to Belgrade for checkups. Me having been wounded myself, I would secure their transportation and they would also receive some per diem money for travel. And that was once or twice a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And where was the veterans' organisation based? Was that in Prijedor town centre?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: Near the market-place. It's still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, in fact, on the basis of the answer that you've just given us, you were not exclusively based at your home but you were in Prijedor town centre once or twice a month for approximately 18 months after you returned from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But, nevertheless, you were not in a position to observe whether over 50.000 non-Serbs had left Prijedor. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: I couldn't notice that. Because nobody moved around Prijedor. Not even the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have any more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you at any other stage, maybe 1995 or later, become aware of the fact that a lot of non-Serbs had moved out of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were rumours to that effect that they had left to western countries across Croatia. Yes, people talked about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Apart from the rumours, did you become aware that they had left, indeed, at some stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So your knowledge is only based on the rumours you heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Even as you sit there now testifying, you're not aware that they left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, any further questions for the witness in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked at temporary transcript page 75, line 22 onwards, if you knew an attack by the VRS upon Stari Grad 30 May 1992. And you gave your answer. And I would like to ask you a related question: When you set out on your route 30 May 1992 to deliver food, had anyone in the Territorial Defence indicated the possibility of any military combat operations anticipated to commence on that day in or near Stari Grad.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN JESIC
utterances.text: No, nobody told me anything. I took over the food in the barracks, and I started touring the fire brigade's hall where I left the food, and then I went to the officers' mess. Nobody told me anything. I drove around unarmed, like before. I had no escorts. I was on my own. And in front of the hall of reserve officers, I saw a dead policeman. Every morning I had been met by those policemen when I brought food. There was nobody. Just that dead policeman. I saw that something was amiss and I returned to the base at the airport, and when I reached the MUP building near the municipality building I saw three or four dead soldiers whose bodies were scattered around the monument to Dr. Mladen Stojanovic. Again, I realised something was amiss. I -- I decided to go in the direction of the grammar school, which is parallel to the main street. I was headed towards the airport. I was ambushed, shot at, and captured. And then I was transferred to the plateau in front of the teachers' school for economics. I was tied. The three of us were tied, Milo Grabovac were [as interpreted] there, and then we were transferred to the machine engineering school where we found two other men who were already there. There were a total of five of us who had been captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we have that in evidence. Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think, as a matter of fact, that after the first line the witness had answered your question, and then you let him go for another 15 lines explaining all kind of things we found already and we heard in the statement. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I thank you again for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes the redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions, Mr. Jeremy? Apparently not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No further questions from the Bench. Mr. Jesic, this concludes your evidence. We'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties, by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber considers it's not very useful to take a break now but, rather, to continue for another 20 minutes or so, and then to perhaps adjourn early for the day. Unless --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have eight minutes left. I think from -- for the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If we would take a break now. That's the reason why the Chamber suggested we should not to take a break and continue to start examination-in-chief of the next witness and then perhaps to have a bit of an early adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are ready to call our next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And your next witness would be, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Our next witness Rato Runjevac, and my colleague Stojanovic will lead him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if I may ask, Your Honours, to have the summary of this witness's statement given to the interpreting booths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, two ushers are busy at this moment to do their jobs. We'll ask them to do that. If you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could -- could one of the ushers assist the Defence in distributing the summary of the witness statement to the various booths. Good afternoon, Mr. Runjevac. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Runjevac. Please be seated. Mr. Runjevac, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You find him standing to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Runjevac, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to slowly pronounce for the transcript your correct first and last name.

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC
utterances.text: Rato Runjevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Runjevac, will you please tell the Trial Chamber if at any point in time you provided a statement to the Defence of General Mladic. Did you provide written answers to questions that were put to you and then, in that sense, draft a written statement as requested from you?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please look at document 65 ter 1D1772 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Runjevac, you should see your statement on the left side of the screen in front of you. My question to you is: Is the signature on this page of the document your signature?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like us to look at the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Runjevac, at the end of the text that we see on this page on the monitor, do we also see your signature and the date written in your own hand?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature; and, yes, that is the date written in my hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Runjevac, while preparing to appear in the courtroom over the past few days, did you tell me that you needed to make a few corrections of typographical errors, and did you need to make some additions in order to make your statement more precise?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to have 65 ter document 1D1772, and could we look at paragraph 2 in that document, i.e., the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Runjevac, did you tell me that the date when you were appointed senior public prosecutor in Sarajevo instead of the 1st of December, 1990, should be the 16th of November, 1990?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at paragraph 16 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Runjevac, did you tell me that for the sake of total precision of your statement, you wanted to make the change --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Stojanovic please tell us where in the paragraph he is making that correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please assist the interpreters by pointing at the precise point where you want to make that correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thus, in paragraph 16, after the word "criminal report to the municipal prosecutor's office," as the witness said, we need to add the Roman numeral II so that the text would read: "To the municipal prosecutor's office II."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. To be more precise, it's the Basic Prosecutor's Office II.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, thank you. And did you not tell me that in the same paragraph, namely, paragraph 16, after the word "the case ended up with investigating judge," and then again you asked for the Roman II to be added so that the text would read: "The case is with the investigative judge of the Basic Court II," and then the rest of the text would remain the same?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 18, Mr. Runjevac, did you not feel the need for the sake of precision to indicate that, in your statement, after the word "where I, with my two children," it should read also: "And my wife." So that the text would read more precisely "where I reside with my two children and my wife," and then the rest of the text would remain the same?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 19, line 2, instead of the date "6th of April, 1992," it should correctly state the "29th of February and the 1st of March, 1992."

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Because this date, the 6th of April, 1992, is the date when Bosnia and Herzegovina received international recognition.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So in the same paragraph, i.e., paragraph 19, did you not point out to me a typographical error in the date where it says: "On Friday, 5th of April, 1992," and then it should correctly read: "On Friday, the 3rd of April, 1992"?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Runjevac, did you not ask the Defence for purposes of precision to add to your statement after the word: "In the safe in my office, I think we have eight pistols and for security reasons, upon the initiative of my deputies, I distributed them," but you wanted to add the words: "And this occurred on the 17th of June, 1991."

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And, finally, in paragraph 21, did you not ask us to correct a typing error in the place where it says: "On the 4th of May, 1992, on Sunday," and instead of that, it should read: "On the 3rd of May, 1992, on a Sunday"?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now that we have made these corrections and additions and, Mr. Runjevac, after you have given the solemn declaration in this courtroom, are you now willing to confirm that if you were asked the same questions today as you were then, you would respond in the same way as you have in the statement, keeping in mind these corrections, and you would stand by what you said regarding the events covered in the statement?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC
utterances.text: Yes. If I may just add something, I worked in the justice system for 41 years. I have given six or seven different oaths, more than a decade -- for more than a decade now I have been a lawyer after also having given the oath. So I do apologise to the Trial Chamber because of these errors because I wrote the statement according to my best recollection while I was on holiday, and then after that before I came for this hearing, I found some minor material evidence and facts which had led me to make these corrections. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Runjevac, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honours, I think that this would be a good moment to admit the witness's statement, the statement of Witness Rato Runjevac, the statement bearing the number 65 ter 1D1772.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document number 1D01772 receives exhibit number D860, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Mr. Stojanovic, I'm looking at the clock. I said we would have an early adjournment today. I don't know how many time you would need for additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or to read the summary. Do you have any additional questions at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my summary is a little bit long but I will have just one question, so I think for all of that, I would need maybe about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the summary and the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would suggest -- one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, we have taken notice of the fact that you have only one question for the witness. If you would put that question to the witness now, we'll hear his answer, and then if you would tomorrow read not a long summary but a short summary of the witness's statement and do that tomorrow. So your one question to the witness, you can put it to him now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, I would like us to look at document D860 in e-court, and then I would like us to focus on paragraph 9 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should be page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Runjevac, you can see paragraph 9 in front of you where, amongst other things, you say that: "At that time, the Croatian and Bosniak deputies, without the Serbian ones, decided in the BH parliament in an unconstitutional way to hold a referendum about the independence of B and H." Could you please tell us why you told the Court this sentence, that this happened in an unconstitutional way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I think this Chamber has heard quite some evidence about what happened on the 14th and the 15th of October. If that is what you're asking about, then we also know that there's -- it's very much in dispute whether this was constitutional or not constitutional. If there's any specific matter this witness could add to what is already in evidence, which highlights both positions, please put a focused question to him and we'll hear his answer. But not in general; it's so repetitious. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will, Your Honour. I believe that we are talking about a very specific element of his legal thesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In short, Mr. Runjevac, could you please tell us what was the legal framework under which you provided your answer or, rather, under which you voiced your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RATO RUNJEVAC
utterances.text: I do not wish to go into the provisions of the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina and amendments to the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, as a witness, I would like to tell the Honourable Chamber that in 1990, as an assistant minister of justice of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I worked on amending the constitution, that I'm the author of Amendment 70, which meant that an old system was transformed into a democratic system. I personally participated in the introduction of some provisions which guaranteed democratic and sovereign rights of all the people and all the peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So when I provided this statement, I remembered that the constitution of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia and Bosnia and Herzegovina did not have a provision allowing for secession. There was just a provision on changing internal borders within the state of SFRY, and I particularly remembered that at that time in order to protect the rights of citizens or, rather, the peoples and national minorities, we incorporated something into Amendment 70 under paragraph 10, and that was the creation of a body whose name was the Council for the Issues of Equality of the Peoples and National Minorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that had to do with all the issues that were decided by the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and those issues were crucial for the national issues of the peoples and national minorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I remember when things started happening between January and May 1992, I participated in those events, and I know that the issue of cessation was against the constitution because pursuant to Amendment 67, the only thing that the parliament could decide on was a change of borders within the SFRY. I also remember that the issue that was put forth before the rump parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina had not undergone a preliminary procedure at the Council for Protection of Constitutionality of the Peoples and National Minorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's why I said that the question that was put at the referendum on the 29th February and the 1st of March, and that was are you in favour of a sovereign and independent state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did not have a legal foundation in constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Runjevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to inform you that that was all I had with this witness, and tomorrow morning I will start with a short summary of the witness's statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's how we will proceed. Mr. Runjevac, we'll resume tomorrow morning. We'd like to see you back at 9.30 in the morning, and I would instruct you not to speak with anyone or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony given today or still to be given tomorrow. You may now follow the usher, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, when you said one question, I was a bit more optimistic about the time it would take. Apologies for that. Apologies to Mr. Mladic as well. Then we adjourn for the day and we will resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 17th of December, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
